transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, thank you. It's nice to meet you. I was actually just telling my neighbor, Susan—she lives in the blue house next door, lovely woman, makes the most incredible lemon bars, though she uses way too much powdered sugar if you ask me—anyway, I was telling her that I’m here because I just can’t seem to turn off the worrying once it starts. 

It’s like a motor that gets stuck. I tell myself, you know, I’ve made the list, I’ve checked the dates on the calendar, I’ve done all I reasonably can do... but my mind just keeps going. Like with my grandson's birthday party last weekend, I had everything planned perfectly. Oh, he just turned seven, and they grow up so fast, don't they? He's completely obsessed with dinosaurs right now, the flying ones especially. I bought him this big pop-up book... 

But yes, what brings me in is just that. Even when everything is handled and checked off, the worrying just doesn't shut off.
Have you ever experienced a sudden feeling of intense fear or discomfort that reached a peak within minutes?

Sudden intense fear? No, I wouldn't say that. It's not really like a sudden shock or a panic or anything. 

Well, speaking of sudden shocks, my husband—rest his soul—used to sneak up on me while I was doing the dishes just to get a jump out of me. He thought it was the funniest thing in the world. We had this beautiful old farmhouse sink in our last house, heavy porcelain, but it was so deep you really had to lean into it to scrub the pots. And he'd come up right behind me and tap my shoulder, and I'd nearly drop whatever I was holding! It's a miracle I never broke any of the good china. 

We have the Royal Doulton set, the Old Country Roses pattern? I don't know if you're familiar, but my mother left it to me. It has that delicate gold banding on the edges, which means you absolutely cannot put it in the dishwasher, no matter what my daughter-in-law says. She completely ruined the gravy boat last Thanksgiving because she just wouldn't listen when I told her the heat would strip the gold right off... 

Oh, but anyway, I'm sorry, my mind is wandering. What was it you asked? Oh, right, the sudden fear. No, it's never really a sudden spike like that. Just that constant hum of worry I was telling you about.
Is your worrying usually about a specific thing or a bunch of different things?

Well, that's just the thing, isn't it? It's never just one thing. It's a whole bunch of different things. My mind just keeps roaming all over the place. Like, one minute I'm fretting over my daughter's travel plans—she's flying out to Seattle next week for a conference, and you know how the weather can get up there this time of year. I keep telling her she needs a proper raincoat, not one of those flimsy windbreakers she insists on wearing. 

And then, before I know it, I'm worrying about whether the house gutters need fixing before the autumn leaves start falling. We have these massive oak trees in the backyard, beautiful in the summer, but oh, the mess they make! My neighbor, Susan—I mentioned her earlier, didn't I?—she had her gutters overflow last year and it caused a terrible leak in her guest bedroom. Ruined a perfectly good antique rug. 

Oh, and then I'm also stressing about the exhibition schedule at the local art gallery where I volunteer on Thursdays. We have a new watercolor collection coming in, and the curator is just terribly disorganized. I swear, if I didn't double-check the shipping manifests, half the paintings would end up in Timbuktu. 

But yes, it's just... everything. It's like all these little things start to feel as if they could unravel into something much bigger, and I just can't seem to stop my brain from jumping from one worry to the next.
Is there one particular area of your life where most of your worries seem to concentrate?

Not really, no. I can't say it's just one area. It really is a little bit of everything. Like just yesterday, I was at the grocery store—the one on Elm Street, not that massive new one out by the highway. That new one is just too overwhelming, and they use those awful, bright LED lights that make all the fruit look completely artificial, don't you think? 

Anyway, I was in the produce section looking for artichokes because my book club is reading a novel set in Italy, and I thought, wouldn't it be lovely to make a proper spinach and artichoke dip from scratch? We're reading *Under the Tuscan Sun*—well, re-reading it, really, because Mary insisted. Mary is the president of the club, and she can be terribly stubborn. She used to be a high school principal, you know, so she still treats the rest of us like we're teenagers caught talking in the hallway... 

Oh, goodness, listen to me rambling. I'm sorry, what were we talking about? Oh, right, my worries. Yes, I was worrying about finding the right artichokes, and then while I was standing right there, I suddenly started worrying about whether the tires on my sedan were getting bald, and then I was fretting about whether I'd remembered to lock the back patio door. So, no, it's not concentrated at all. It just sort of... latches onto whatever is in front of me.
Do you feel like your worrying is interfering with your daily life or activities?

Well, it's not like I'm completely housebound or anything. I still keep up with the garden, and of course, my book club. I wouldn't miss book club, even with Mary being so demanding. Although... I have noticed I've started arriving less prepared lately. I didn't even finish the last three chapters of the book last week, which is so unlike me. 

And you know, I've actually started turning down parts of the exhibition planning at the gallery, too. It just feels harder to manage than it used to. The curator—oh, I mentioned her earlier, didn't I? She wanted me to coordinate the opening night reception for the watercolor exhibit. Now, usually, I love doing that. I have this wonderful caterer, Antonio, he makes the most divine little bruschettas. But this time, just thinking about coordinating Antonio and the wine deliveries and making sure the lighting was right... it just felt so heavy. 

Speaking of lighting, they finally fixed the streetlamp outside my bedroom window. It was flickering for weeks! I must have called the city council three times. You'd think with the property taxes we pay in this neighborhood, they could change a lightbulb faster than a month, wouldn't you? The woman on the phone—Brenda, I think her name was—she sounded so bored every time I called. 

But anyway... what was I saying? Oh, right, the gallery. Yes, I just told them I couldn't handle the reception this time. It's just... it's all feeling a bit harder to juggle than it used to.
Do you feel like your worrying is causing you a lot of distress?

Distress? Well, yes, it is quite upsetting. Like I was just mentioning a moment ago, it really bothers me that I'm having to step back from things. I mean, I’m still keeping up with the garden and going to the book club, but realizing I'm arriving less prepared and having to turn down that exhibition planning... it just feels so much harder to manage everything than it used to, and that makes me feel awful. I used to be the one everyone relied on! 

At least the garden gets me outside, which is a small mercy. Oh, you should see my hydrangeas right now. They are absolutely spectacular this year. Did you know you can change their color from pink to blue just by adding coffee grounds or aluminum sulfate to the soil? It's all about the pH levels. I get my soil supplies from this lovely little nursery on 4th Street. Mr. Henderson runs it—he must be nearly ninety by now, bless his heart. He always wears these funny little suspenders with embroidered tomatoes on them. I asked him where he got them once, and he said his granddaughter made them for his birthday years ago... 

Oh, listen to me going on again. I'm sorry. But yes, to answer your question, it is very distressing. It's just terribly frustrating feeling like my normal routines are suddenly too heavy to carry.
How long have you been experiencing this constant worrying?

Well, it's been about seven months now. It all really started shortly after my dear friend passed away. I was just trying so hard to keep all our little projects moving forward, you know? We had so many things we were working on together. 

Actually, she was the one who first got me into the gallery work I was telling you about. Her name was Eleanor. Oh, Eleanor had the most exquisite taste. She could walk into a thrift store and find a genuine mid-century vase just sitting there between a pile of old paperbacks and a broken toaster. We used to go antique hunting every second Sunday of the month. There was this one shop out in the valley, an old barn they converted—it always smelled faintly of lavender and old paper. The owner, a man named Arthur, had this enormous ginger cat that would just drape itself across the display cases like a furry scarf. You had to be so careful not to wake him when you wanted to look at the jewelry. 

I bought a lovely silver brooch there once, shaped like a dragonfly. I wore it to Eleanor’s funeral, actually. It just felt right. 

But, oh, I'm wandering off again, aren't I? I apologize. But yes, to answer your question, it's been about seven months of this constant worrying, ever since I tried taking over all those things we used to do together.
Is there anything in particular that you worry about more than other things?

Well, you'd think there would be one big thing, wouldn't you? But it's not really like that. My mind just keeps roaming all over the place. Like, I'll be stressing over that exhibition schedule I was just telling you about, and then suddenly I'm fretting over my daughter's travel plans. 

She's going to Italy, you see. Florence. It's a beautiful city, but I told her, "Sarah, you have to watch out for pickpockets near the Duomo." I read this article in a magazine at the dentist's office—Dr. Evans always has those nice glossy travel magazines, though his waiting room chairs are dreadfully uncomfortable. Anyway, the article said thieves use these little razor blades to slice right through the bottom of your leather purse! I actually bought her one of those special anti-theft bags with the wire mesh hidden inside, but she said it looked too "sensible." Can you imagine? She bought this bright yellow suede thing instead. Yellow! One drop of espresso and it's completely ruined. 

But... oh, what was I saying? Right, the worrying. So I'll be thinking about her trip, and then my brain just jumps right over to whether the house gutters need fixing before the autumn rains. The oak tree in the front yard drops so many leaves, and the boy from down the street who usually cleans them out for me just went off to college. 

So, no, it's not one particular thing. It's just that all these small things start to feel as if they could unravel into something much, much bigger. It just never seems to stop roaming from one thing to the next.
Is there ever a time when you feel like you're not worrying about anything at all?

Well, I wish I could say there was. That's actually what brings me in today, to be honest. I just can't seem to turn off the worrying once it starts. I'll tell myself, "Helen, you've made the list, you've checked all the dates, you've done everything you reasonably can," but the thoughts just keep spinning. 

It's like this new recipe organizer I bought last week. I thought, if I just get all my recipes in order, I won't worry so much about what to make for the book club luncheons. I used to just keep them all in this old tin box—it was a beautiful tin, actually, from a shortbread company in Scotland. My husband and I went to Edinburgh for our 25th anniversary, and we bought it at this little shop right on the Royal Mile. The shortbread was terribly dry, but the tin had these lovely embossed thistles on it. Anyway, I bought this new binder with the clear plastic sleeves, thinking it would help me feel more organized. I spent three hours sorting my appetizers from my mains, but then I just started worrying about whether the plastic sleeves were archival quality and if the ink on my grandmother's pound cake recipe would fade. 

Grandma always used this beautiful blue fountain pen ink. You just don't see penmanship like hers anymore. They don't teach cursive in schools now, do they? My grandson was trying to read a birthday card I sent him, and he had to ask his mother to translate it for him! It's a shame, really. 

But... oh dear, I've lost the thread again. What I mean is, even when I try to be proactive and get things sorted out, the worrying just latches onto something else. I just can't seem to make it stop, no matter how much I try to reason with myself.
Are you finding it harder to spend time with friends or family because of your worrying?

Well, I still see them. I still keep up with the garden and my book club. Oh, the book club is quite the affair, usually. We're reading this enormous biography of Winston Churchill right now. It's fascinating, really, but the book itself is so incredibly heavy! I tried reading it in bed the other night and dropped it right on my nose. My husband used to say I shouldn't read in bed anyway because the reading lamp bothers him, but he's one to talk, always falling asleep in his armchair with those old Westerns blaring. You know, John Wayne, Clint Eastwood... you just can't get him to watch anything else on a Sunday afternoon. 

But... oh, I'm doing it again, aren't I? I'm sorry. You asked about seeing people. So, yes, I still go to the book club, but I've started arriving much less prepared lately. I just haven't been finishing the chapters. And that exhibition planning I was telling you about earlier? I've actually started turning down parts of it. 

Which is a real shame, because we have this lovely young watercolorist coming in next month who paints the most beautiful local birds. Cardinals, blue jays... he uses this thick, imported textured paper that just soaks up the color perfectly. I really wanted to curate his whole display. But... well, I just had to step back from it. It just feels so much harder to manage all those moving parts than it used to.
Are you finding that your worrying is affecting your ability to work or take care of daily responsibilities?

Well, I suppose I just mentioned that, didn't I? About the exhibition and the book club. I mean, I still do them. I still keep up with my garden, too. My hydrangeas are absolutely spectacular this year. I switched to a new fertilizer—it's organic, made from kelp, if you can believe it. The woman at the nursery swore by it. She has this lovely little shop out on County Road 9, and she always wears these huge straw hats with ribbons. I bought one myself, actually, to keep the sun off my face while I'm weeding, but the brim is so wide I keep knocking it into the trellis where my climbing roses are. 

Those roses... they really need pruning, now that I think of it. My husband used to do the heavy pruning, but his arthritis has been acting up. He takes that glucosamine stuff, but I don't know if it really works. 

Oh, right, my responsibilities. Yes, well, like I was saying before, I still go to the book club and tend the garden, but... I just show up less prepared. I haven't been finishing the books. And the exhibition planning... I just had to turn down parts of it. Managing all those moving parts, it just feels so much harder than it used to. I just don't have the energy for it when my mind is always spinning.
Is your worrying usually centered around a few specific topics or is it more scattered across many different areas of your life?

Well, it's really all over the place, if I'm being honest. My mind just keeps roaming from one thing to the next. Like, I'll be worrying about the exhibition schedule, and then suddenly I'm fretting about my daughter's travel plans. She's going to Italy next month, you know. Tuscany. She rented this little villa that looks just charming in the pictures, but you know how those online listings can be. Remember that time we rented a cabin in the Poconos and the "rustic charm" turned out to mean no indoor plumbing? My husband was furious. He had to trudge out in the snow every morning just to... well, anyway, she says it has a pool, but I keep thinking, what if the pool pump breaks? Or what if she loses her passport on the train? I bought her one of those money belts you wear under your clothes, but she says they're unfashionable. Unfashionable! As if the pickpockets in Rome care about fashion. 

And then, while I'm worrying about her passport, I'll suddenly remember the house gutters. They really need fixing before the autumn rains start. The oak tree in the front yard drops so many leaves, and last year they got all clogged up and water started pooling near the foundation. We had to hire that nice young man, Tommy, from down the street to clean them out. He's grown so tall! He used to come over for Halloween dressed as a little pirate, and now he's off to college. Studying engineering, his mother said. I hope he does well, engineering sounds so difficult with all that math...

Oh, dear, I've wandered off again. I'm sorry. What I mean is, it's not just one thing. It's the exhibition, my daughter, the gutters... it's like all these small things just start to feel as if they could unravel into something much bigger, and my brain just bounces between them all day long.
Do you often feel restless or on edge when you're worrying?

Well, yes, I suppose I do. I feel very wound up a lot of the time, even just sitting in my own living room. I'll be on the phone with my sister—she lives out in Oregon now, near Portland. It rains there constantly, but she claims she loves it. She actually started raising alpacas a few years ago. Can you imagine? My sister, who used to refuse to wear anything but dry-clean-only silk blouses, out there shearing alpacas in the mud. She sent me a scarf made from their wool for Christmas. It's incredibly soft, really, a lovely shade of oatmeal, but it sheds everywhere. I wore it over my navy peacoat once and looked like I'd been rolling around with a golden retriever. We had a golden retriever when the girls were little, Buster, and he was just the sweetest thing, but the vacuuming... 

Oh, right, being on edge. Yes, well, when I'm on the phone with her, or anyone really, I find I can't just sit still. I'm always tapping my fingers on the armrest, or I have to get up and straighten a picture frame or fluff the pillows. Sitting quietly just makes me feel so jumpy lately, like I have to be moving or doing something, even when there's nothing that actually needs doing.
Are your worries usually about everyday, routine kinds of things?

Well, yes, I suppose they are. Just normal, everyday things. Nothing terribly dramatic, just... routine. Like going to the grocery store, or the bank. Actually, speaking of the bank, they just remodeled the branch on Main Street and it is completely unrecognizable. They took out all the proper teller windows and put in these little futuristic pods. You just stand there right next to the person while they type. It feels terribly informal, doesn't it? 

I was in there Tuesday trying to deposit a check, and the young man at the pod—he couldn't have been older than twenty, he actually still had braces—he kept trying to convince me to deposit it using the camera on my mobile phone. I told him, I don't want a picture of my money floating around on my phone, what if I lose it? I lose my phone all the time. Just last week I found it in the refrigerator sitting right on top of the crisper drawer. I was putting away some celery and just set it down without thinking. Celery has gotten so expensive lately, by the way. Three dollars for a bunch that was mostly just limp leaves! I was going to make a Waldorf salad for the book club, but with prices like that, I ended up just making a nice potato salad instead. My mother's recipe, with a little dash of paprika on top. 

Oh, dear me. I'm doing it again, aren't I? I'm so sorry, my mind just runs away with me. But yes, to answer your question, I'm not worrying about the end of the world or anything grand like that. It really is just the usual, everyday sort of things.
Is there a particular aspect of your life where you feel your worrying is most prominent?

Well, I wouldn't say there's one specific part of my life that takes up most of the worry. It really just... everything gets its turn, I suppose. I mean, I do fret about the gallery a lot—I help organize the local art exhibitions, as I mentioned. We have the spring watercolor showcase coming up, and watercolors are just terribly unforgiving. My friend Martha actually tried to take up watercolor painting a couple of years ago. She bought all these expensive sable brushes from a specialty catalog. They were shipped all the way from France, took absolutely weeks to arrive. And the very first day she sat down to paint a little bowl of lemons, her cat, Mr. Whiskers—he's this enormous Maine Coon, just a massive ball of fluff—jumped right onto the dining table and knocked the muddy paint water all over her paper. And the floor! It completely stained her oak hardwood. She had to buy a rug just to cover it up. A Persian rug, very pretty, mostly burgundy, though I always think burgundy makes a room look a bit dark. I much prefer lighter colors, like a nice soft sage green. I painted my guest room sage green last spring and it really opened the space up. 

But, oh dear, listen to me. A particular aspect? No, I really couldn't pick just one area. It's not just the gallery or my family or the house, it just hops around from one ordinary thing to another.
Do you often find yourself feeling restless or fidgety when you're not actively worrying about something?

Well, I suppose I do. Like I was saying earlier, I just feel so wound up, even when I'm just sitting in my own living room. I'll be on the phone with someone, and even if we're just talking about nothing at all, nothing to worry over, I can't just sit there. I'm tapping my fingers on the armrest, or I have to stand up and straighten a picture frame. We have this lovely silver frame on the mantel, it holds a picture of my husband and me from a trip we took to Charleston years ago. Oh, Charleston is just beautiful in the spring, the jasmine smells absolutely heavenly. We took a carriage ride through the historic district, and the horse was named Buttercup. Such a sweet horse, but she had this terrible habit of stopping to try and eat the hedges right out of people's front yards! The driver had to keep pulling her along. I felt a bit sorry for her, really, the hedges did look quite green and fresh. 

But yes, even if I'm just looking at that picture frame, I have to get up and make sure it's perfectly straight, or I start fluffing the pillows on the sofa. Sitting quietly just makes me feel so jumpy, like my motor is running even when I'm not actively worrying about a single thing.
Are you finding that your worrying is affecting your relationships with family or friends?

Well, my friends haven't said anything directly to me, really. I do still keep up with my garden and the book club, so I am still seeing everyone. Oh, the garden is practically a full-time job right now, though. The aphids have been absolutely dreadful this year on my roses. I tried spraying them with a little mixture of dish soap and water—I read about it in a magazine at the hair salon. My hairdresser, Betty, always keeps the best magazines in her waiting area, not just those silly celebrity tabloids, but proper home and garden ones. 

Anyway, Betty just had her first grandchild last month, a little boy named Oliver. Such a lovely, traditional name, don't you think? So many people are naming their children after fruits and random cities these days, it's terribly confusing. I met a little girl at the park named Apple once, can you imagine? Her mother kept calling out "Apple! Apple, don't eat the sand!" and I spent a good minute looking around for a piece of dropped fruit before I realized she meant the child. 

But... oh, I'm wandering off again, aren't I? I'm sorry. You asked about my relationships. Well, like I said, I still go to the book club, but I’ve started arriving much less prepared lately. I just haven't been finishing the chapters. And with the exhibition planning at the gallery, I’ve actually started turning down parts of it. Taking on the organizing just feels so much harder to manage than it used to.
Have you noticed any significant problems at work, at home, or in your relationships due to your worrying?

Well, I suppose I kind of just mentioned this, didn't I? My mind is just... well, it's a bit all over the place. But yes, I'd say the worrying is definitely making things harder. I mean, I'm still doing things, of course. I haven't just shut myself away. I still keep up with the garden, which, as I said, the aphids are just relentless. And I still go to my book club every other Tuesday. We meet at Eleanor's house usually, because she has that lovely sunroom. Oh, her sunroom is just gorgeous, especially in the late afternoon when the light catches all her stained glass suncatchers. She makes them herself, you know. Takes little pieces of sea glass she finds on her trips to the coast. Her husband, Richard, used to complain about all the buckets of glass she'd bring home in the trunk of the car, but now he helps her polish them. He bought her this little tumbler machine for Christmas two years ago. It’s quite loud, though, sounds like a washing machine full of rocks, which I suppose is exactly what it is. I could never have something that noisy in my house, it would set my teeth on edge.

But, oh, right, the problems. Well, even though I still go to the book club, I've started arriving much less prepared. I just... I haven't been finishing the chapters. I read a page and realize I haven't absorbed a single word because I'm fretting about something else. And with the gallery, the exhibition planning... I've actually started turning down parts of it. I told them I couldn't handle the catering coordination this time. Taking on the organizing just feels so much harder to manage than it used to. It's just all a bit much.
Are you finding that your worrying is significantly interfering with your ability to enjoy or participate in activities you normally like to do?

Well, I suppose it is a bit, yes. Like I was just saying, I do still force myself to go out and do things. I haven't completely stopped, you know. I still have my garden, and the book club... though, as I mentioned, I just haven't been keeping up with the reading. I sit down with the book and my mind just races. We're reading a historical fiction right now, set in 1920s Paris. Oh, Paris in the twenties! Can you imagine? All those wonderful writers and artists just bumping into each other at cafes. Hemingway, Fitzgerald... though I read a biography of Zelda Fitzgerald once, and goodness, they had a terribly complicated marriage. So much drama. I suppose that's what happens when two very passionate, creative people try to live together. My husband and I are much more boring, thank goodness. He was an accountant before he retired. Very steady, very predictable. He likes his dinner at exactly six o'clock every evening. We usually have chicken on Tuesdays. 

But... oh dear, I'm doing it again, aren't I? I apologize. What were we talking about? Oh, right, enjoying things. Well, it's just that I’m not getting the same joy out of things because I'm so distracted. Like the book club, arriving unprepared. And the gallery... I used to love helping with the exhibition planning, but I've had to start turning parts of it down. It just feels so much harder to manage everything now. It's like I don't have the mental energy for it anymore.

Speaking of lighting, they finally fixed the streetlamp outside my bedroom window. It was flickering for weeks! I must have called the city council three times. You'd think with the property taxes we pay in this neighborhood, they could change a lightbulb faster than a month, wouldn't you? The woman on the phone—Brenda, I think her name was—she sounded so bored every time I called. 

But anyway... what was I saying? Oh, right, the gallery. Yes, I just told them I couldn't handle the reception this time. It's just... it's all feeling a bit harder to juggle than it used to.

Well, I wish I could say there was. That's actually what brings me in today, to be honest. I just can't seem to turn off the worrying once it starts. I'll tell myself, "Helen, you've made the list, you've checked all the dates, you've done everything you reasonably can," but the thoughts just keep spinning. 

It's like this new recipe organizer I bought last week. I thought, if I just get all my recipes in order, I won't worry so much about what to make for the book club luncheons. I used to just keep them all in this old tin box—it was a beautiful tin, actually, from a shortbread company in Scotland. My husband and I went to Edinburgh for our 25th anniversary, and we bought it at this little shop right on the Royal Mile. The shortbread was terribly dry, but the tin had these lovely embossed thistles on it. Anyway, I bought this new binder with the clear plastic sleeves, thinking it would help me feel more organized. I spent three hours sorting my appetizers from my mains, but then I just started worrying about whether the plastic sleeves were archival quality and if the ink on my grandmother's pound cake recipe would fade. 

Grandma always used this beautiful blue fountain pen ink. You just don't see penmanship like hers anymore. They don't teach cursive in schools now, do they? My grandson was trying to read a birthday card I sent him, and he had to ask his mother to translate it for him! It's a shame, really. 

But... oh dear, I've lost the thread again. What I mean is, even when I try to be proactive and get things sorted out, the worrying just latches onto something else. I just can't seem to make it stop, no matter how much I try to reason with myself.
